title: Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board
intro: This guide explains what Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 says about who it covers, the role of the Landlord and Tenant Board, repairs, rent deposits, ending a tenancy and applications to the Board. It describes the Act generally and does not say how it applies to any particular tenancy.

sections.heading: What the Act covers
paragraphs: Except for Part V.1, the Act says it “applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.” A “rental unit” means “any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises”. It includes “a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 2 (1), 3 (1))

A “tenancy agreement” means “a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit”. Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, “a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 2 (1), 4 (1))
If the Act conflicts with another Act, the Act applies, with one exception: “other than the Human Rights Code”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 3 (4))

sections.heading: Housing the Act does not cover
paragraphs: Section 5 lists kinds of living accommodation the Act “does not apply with respect to”. Examples include accommodation for “the travelling or vacationing public” in places such as hotels, motels and campgrounds, and “short-term living accommodation provided as emergency shelter”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 5 (a), (f))

Another listed exemption is accommodation where the occupant is “required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner's spouse, child or parent or the spouse's child or parent”, and that person “lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”. The full list in section 5 has more categories, such as certain student housing and farm-employment housing. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 5 (b), (g), (i))

Commercial tenancies fall under a different law. The Commercial Tenancies Act says: “This Act does not apply to tenancies and tenancy agreements to which the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.” (Commercial Tenancies Act, s. 2)

sections.heading: The Landlord and Tenant Board
paragraphs: The Act continues the former tribunal “under the name Landlord and Tenant Board”. It says: “The Board has exclusive jurisdiction to determine all applications under this Act and with respect to all matters in which jurisdiction is conferred on it by this Act.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 168 (1), (2))
The Board “has authority to hear and determine all questions of law and fact with respect to all matters within its jurisdiction under this Act.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 174)

Tribunals Ontario describes the Board as the place to “Resolve a dispute with a landlord or tenant, and/or end a tenancy or co-op member’s occupancy”. Its page says the Tribunals Ontario Portal can be used to “submit applications, check file status, upload evidence and use the dispute resolution tool to try and reach an agreement.” (Tribunals Ontario, Landlord and Tenant Board)

sections.heading: Money limits and going to court
paragraphs: Where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, the Board may order payment “of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (1))

A person entitled to apply under the Act “but whose claim exceeds the Board's monetary jurisdiction may commence a proceeding in any court of competent jurisdiction”. The court may then exercise any powers the Board could have exercised. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (2))

If a party claims an amount at or below the Board's limit, “all rights of the party in excess of the Board's monetary jurisdiction are extinguished once the Board issues its order.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (3))

sections.heading: Repairs and maintenance
paragraphs: Under the Act, “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.” This applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair, or of “a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 20 (1), (2))

If the Board determines on a tenant's application that a landlord breached this obligation, the orders it may make include to “Terminate the tenancy”, “Order an abatement of rent”, and “Order the landlord to do specified repairs or replacements or other work within a specified time.” The full list is in section 30. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 30 (1))

sections.heading: Rent deposits
paragraphs: The Act says: “The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.” A landlord may require a rent deposit “if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 105 (1), 106 (1))

The deposit “shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.” The landlord “shall pay interest to the tenant annually” on the deposit at the rent increase guideline rate. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 106 (2), (6))

A landlord “shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 106 (10))

sections.heading: Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds
paragraphs: The Act says: “A tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act.” A notice of termination must be in a form approved by the Board (or a prescribed form), and must identify the rental unit, state the termination date, and be signed by the person giving it or that person's agent. A landlord's notice must also “set out the reasons and details respecting the termination”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 37 (1), 43)

A landlord's notice must tell the tenant that if the tenant does not move out, “the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant”, and that “the tenant is entitled to dispute the application.” A tenant may end a tenancy at the end of a period or term by giving notice under section 44. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 43 (2), 47)

Grounds on which the Act lets a landlord give notice include: non-payment of rent; persistent late payment; an illegal act; undue damage; substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; an act that seriously impairs safety; more people living in the unit than health, safety or housing standards allow; and the landlord, a family member or a purchaser requiring the unit in good faith for residential occupation. Each ground has its own conditions in the section that sets it out. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 48, 49, 58 to 67)

A landlord may also give notice if the landlord requires possession of the rental unit to “demolish it”, to “convert it to use for a purpose other than residential premises”, or to do repairs or renovations “that are so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 50 (1))

For these notices, the termination date “shall be at least 120 days after the notice is given and shall be the day a period of the tenancy ends or, where the tenancy is for a fixed term, the end of the term.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 50 (2))

sections.heading: Applications to the Board and their time limits
paragraphs: A tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for the orders listed in section 29, about: the landlord's repair obligation; withholding or deliberately interfering with the reasonable supply of a vital service, care service or food; substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference by the landlord, superintendent or agent; altering the locking system without giving replacement keys; and illegal entry. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 29 (1))

For these tenant applications, “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 29 (2))

A landlord who has given notice may apply for “an order terminating a tenancy and evicting the tenant”. That application “may not be made later than 30 days after the termination date specified in the notice”, but this does not apply to an application based on failure to pay rent. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 69 (1), (2), (3))

A landlord may also apply for an order that a tenant or former tenant pay arrears of rent, or pay reasonable repair or replacement costs where the tenant, another occupant or a person the tenant permitted there wilfully or negligently caused undue damage. Each may be made “while the tenant is in possession of the rental unit” or “no later than one year after the tenant or former tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 87 (1), (1.1), 89 (1), (1.1))
